en: Prosperity!
An Exposition of One's Own Self
I worship the pair of feet of the venerable Guru, which have churned away the unbearable pairs of opposites;
whose ashes, having extinguished the dust of the grasping of delusion, spread everywhere. 1.1.
I salute the compassionate and supreme guide who has destroyed all doubts, whose pair of feet teaches the non-dual experience that is the meaning of that state. 1.2.
Scorched by the forest fire of saṃsāra, the disciple—equipped with all the necessary means—is awakened by the teacher through words skillful in defining one's own self. (1.3)
Who among men has any doubt regarding the fact that "I exist"?
If there were doubt even in this matter, you yourself would be the one who doubted.
He who knows "I am not" truly knows that Brahman does not exist;
he who realizes "I am" knows Brahman by himself as his very own self. 1.5.
"Brahminhood is indeed that [Self]; therefore, 'I am not a Brahmin' is merely delusion.
Through delusion duality arises; all afflictions have their root in that. (1.6)
Having attained seclusion from the five sheaths, this [mind] does not associate with the five afflictions;
for this very reason, those of virtuous intellect constantly investigate the five sheaths. (1.7)

Through discernment, the Self attains its true luminosity by distinguishing itself from the five sheaths— consisting of food, vital breath, mind, consciousness, and bliss— which each possess a progressively greater degree of subtlety.
This body, known as the "sheath composed of food," is not the Self; it is insentient and comparable to a jar, because it is observed to exist prior to birth and to cease to exist after death. (1.9)
This sheath consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya) is a particular kind of air delimited within the body;
how could it be the Self when it is subject to the affliction of hunger and thirst? (1.10)
That which conceives "I-ness" toward the body and "mine-ness" toward the home and so forth,
being subject to passion and aversion— that is not the Self, but the sheath composed of mind (manomaya-kośa).
In sleep, it is itself dissolved; in waking, it pervades the entire body.
That which is denoted by the term "consciousness" (vijñāna) is the reflection of consciousness (cit), not the intellect (buddhi), nor even the self (ātman). 1.12
How could that egoism, which identifies itself as "I am happy" based on the mere fragments of pleasure found in deep sleep, be the Self—this egoism known as the "sheath of bliss"? (1.13)
That which manifests as the reflected image is indeed the bliss that is the self of all;
for it exists prior to and after [the state of manifestation], and because it is unchanging and unsublatable. (1.14)

If nothing other than this [self] consisting of food and so forth is experienced, there is no denial whatsoever of the fact that there exists an experiencer of that which consists of food and the rest. (1.15)

Although this [consciousness] cannot be an object of experience because it is itself the experiencer, there can never be any suspicion of its non-existence, since its existence is the very nature of awareness itself. (1.16)
The Self experiences the universe through the universe, yet it is not experienced [as an object];
indeed, the sun, while illuminating the entire universe, is not itself illuminated.

That which cannot be described as "this," "such," "like this," "to such an extent," or "just that much"—that is to be understood as Brahman; otherwise, it would be an object and would be beyond perception.
Even though everything perceived as "this, this" is everywhere sublated, the reality that is not "this" remains unsublated; because it exists, it is not something beyond perception.
The Brahman is not unknown or beyond perception, because it is self-luminous.
Its definition is proclaimed as: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. (1.20)
When the limiting conditions of the treasury and power exist, it manifests as the Lord of the living beings;
if not, then due to the absence of those two, it shines in its own essential nature, free from all distinctions.

If it is established by worldly experience that when all objects of perception are sublated, nothing at all exists, then that which is established as "nothing at all" is itself established by the Veda as Brahman. (1.22)
Thus, for those devoid of discernment, through the contemplation of such statements as "That thou art," this Self appears as if remote, even though it is shining forth directly. 1.23.

Therefore, by first purifying the meaning of the constituent words and then contemplating the meaning of the sentence, one realizes the Self directly in an instant through the power of the Guru’s compassion. 1.24.

The referent of the word "thou" (tvaṃpada) is that consciousness which, superimposing the attributes of the body, senses, and so forth upon the Self as non-different from it, possesses the conceit of being an agent and the like. (1.25)
That consciousness which manifests as the witness of the body and the senses, being distinct from them, is declared to be the indicated meaning (lakṣya-artha) of the term "thou" (tvaṃpada). 1.26.

The meaning expressed by the word "That" (tat) is consciousness, which is to be known through the words of the conclusion of the Vedas, which is the material cause of the entire universe, and which is endowed with omniscience and other such qualities. 1.27.

Consciousness, which is free from diverse limiting adjuncts, transcends the universe, pure, non-dual, imperishable, and knowable through direct experience—that is the indicated meaning of the word "That" (tat). 1.28.
First there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), followed by the relation of qualifier and qualified;
then there arises the relationship between the denotata and the indicator, which constitutes the connection between the natures of the word-meanings. (1.29)

"Experts in linguistic interpretation (lākṣaṇika) state that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) occurs when words whose grounds for application are distinct have their application in a single object. (1.30)
Inwardness, immediacy, fullness, and being accompanied by a second are mutually contradictory; therefore, in this context, one must necessarily resort to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). 1.31.

When the primary meaning cannot be accepted due to its contradiction by another means of valid cognition, that function which applies to a meaning inseparable from the primary one is called *lakṣaṇā* (indication). 1.32.

Alternatively, "exclusive" (jahatī) indication would be that in which the function [of a word], having abandoned its entire denoted meaning, resides in another meaning associated with it; this is not to be accepted here, as in the case of "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā. (1.33)

That function of a word which proceeds toward another meaning without abandoning its primary (literal) meaning is called *ajahat-svārthā* (non-abandoning its own sense); however, in this context, it is not to be accepted, as in the example "The red [horse] runs. (1.34)

That [function] which, having abandoned one part of the denoted meaning, causes another part to be understood, would be called *jahadajahatī* (the abandoning-non-abandoning); one should resort to this [function], as in the case of the expression "that same twice-born man" (*so 'yaṃ dvijaḥ*). (1.35)

This very sentence, "He is that twice-born man," having abandoned the distinctions of proximity, remoteness, place, and so forth, because it characterizes the mere essence of the twice-born, expresses the identity of both referents. (1.36)

Similarly, in the statement "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), having set aside the qualities of being remote and immediate and so forth, it indicates the reality of consciousness and makes the identity clear through the word "thou" (asi). || 1.37 ||
Thus, by means of a great statement that demonstrates unity, the Veda makes known the state free from sorrow to those who directly perceive the meaning thus awakened as "I. (1.38)
In both worldly and Vedic usage, it is observed that injunctive statements generally function as instigators to action.
How, then, could this be the case for such [statements] as "That thou art," which merely inform one of an already established fact? (1.39)
Even the cognition of a desired object does not by itself produce activity; it is destiny alone that impels action.
People proceed to act upon the realization that "the king is coming" or "a son has been born. (1.40)
Although the Self is constantly being revealed by the Vedic texts whose sole purpose is unity, it cannot be directly perceived by persons who lack the compassion of a spiritual teacher. 1.41

One who has abandoned both desired and forbidden actions, whose mind is purified by the performance of prescribed duties, and who resorts to his own innate consciousness—should it not be considered by you that such a person is indeed a guru? 1.42
Enlightenment does not arise through actions alone without a teacher who is a treasure-house of compassion;
for the meaning that "a person possessing a teacher knows" is established by the Vedas. (1.43)
The Veda is the supreme authority, whether by virtue of its beginninglessness or because it was composed by the Supreme Lord; there is no sublation of it, either from itself or from another. 1.44.

That statement of the Vedas which does not depend on anything else, whereas all other means of knowledge depend upon it—that is the authority for the perception of supersensuous objects beyond the Brāhmaṇas and other sources. 1.45.
Those great-souled ones who seek to understand awakening by means of pride, while that very pride is awakening it, are like those who desire to burn fire with fuel. 1.46.
The Veda is beginningless; its manifester is the Lord, whose nature is self-luminous.
Having observed its manifestation by Him, the wise have declared it to be a means of valid knowledge. (1.47)
Just as no other cause for the perception of forms is seen than the eye, so too, in the cognition of the unseen [dharma], there is no other means of knowing it than the Veda. (1.48)

If someone reveals in a tantra that which has already been determined in meaning within the Vedic scriptures (nigama), this is merely a restatement; no authority whatsoever is established for it. 1.49
In the Veda, which possesses two parts, one part establishes duality alone, while another well-known part propounds non-duality as the very reality. (1.50)
Non-duality alone is real; within it, duality is not real, being superimposed like silver upon mother-of-pearl, or like the appearance of water in a mirage. (1.51)
If non-duality were superimposed upon the reality of duality—which is unreal—that would be entirely improper, because superimposition of unreal things occurs only upon that which is real. (1.52)

If superimposition applies to both [subject and object], it is because there is nothing else apart from them; yet superimposition does not occur in the void. Therefore, the reality of non-duality must be accepted. (1.53)
Non-duality, which is not apprehended through perception and other means of knowledge, is that which must be established by scripture;
duality is not to be established, because it is already established in the world by its very nature. 1.54
Non-duality is the nature of bliss, whereas duality is always unbearable suffering;
the Śruti teaches only that for which there is a purpose. 1.55.

Some maintain that the innate nature of that [Self], which is the non-dual reality consisting of bliss and is the subject to be established by the words of the Vedas, is the state of being a living soul (jīvatva). 1.56.
If the state of being a living being belonged to that clear consciousness by its very nature, it could never undergo destruction, just as heat and light do not leave the fire. (1.57)

Just as iron pierced by mercury attains the state of gold, in that very same way, some maintain that this individual soul (jīva) attains the state of the Supreme through the power of the means of realization. 1.58.

Therefore, this is not logical: once that [refinement] has long since passed away, even the golden color, having been joined with iron, undergoes destruction when its flavor and potency are lost. (1.59)

Likewise, this state of being a living soul, though endowed with various characteristics of pleasure and pain, appears as if it has already passed away through the power of its causal means; yet it proceeds without undergoing destruction.
Therefore, if the individual soul (jīva) existed by its own nature, it would always remain that very soul;
likewise, if the Supreme Self (paramātman) were this [soul], it would logically follow that this is indeed the Supreme Self. (1.61)
Or if the living soul attains equality with another through the power of spiritual practice, it is certain that even that will surely perish after some period of time; so all agree. (1.62)
Therefore, having swallowed one's own body and this delusive cycle of worldly existence by means of self-knowledge, the Self alone remains as the full reality; nothing else remains.
All the Śrutis, together with all the Smṛtis, teach that which is truth, knowledge, infinite, the primordial nature, the form of the Supreme Self, and non-dual. (1.64)
All other scriptural statements are declared to be supplementary to this [text], which consists of the entire network of Vedic sentences that teach non-duality. 1.65.
When [the knowledge] has arisen like the sun, agency and other such notions depart like darkness;
how then can that non-dual knowledge arise from such [Vedic statements] as "That thou art"? (1.66)
Knowledge that culminates within the section on ritual action is held by the wise to be an auxiliary part of action;
how could knowledge, which belongs to a different section, become an auxiliary to action? (1.67)
The two sections consist respectively of ritual action and knowledge, distinguished by their respective qualifications and subjects.
This being so, how can there be a mutual relationship of subsidiary and principal between these two? (1.68)
Knowledge would not exist in action, and likewise this action would not exist in knowledge;
how then can the combination of these two be possible, like light and darkness? (1.69)
Therefore, when delusion has ceased, knowledge does not require any other assistance, just as the sun does not require a companion in order to utterly destroy a dense mass of darkness. (1.70)
Thus, that stainless knowledge becomes the Supreme Self, the witness of the universe;
as such, it is not bound by those very attributes, being existence-consciousness-bliss. (1.71)
Its connection with the visible world is like the relationship between a rope and a snake;
the scripture also establishes this very point by stating that "this [Self] is eternally unattached. (1.72)
That for which both agent and object manifest within the heart does not know itself;
whereas that for which neither agent nor object exists is what truly advances toward being known with perfect clarity. (1.73)
"Agency and all such [attributes] are acquired entirely through the power of māyā"; thus some say, "This is merely delusion arising from an excess of ignorance, and nothing else. (1.74)
When that Brahman is known, this entire universe becomes known without exception;
just as when the causal clay is known, the jar, the water-pot, and so forth are understood. || 1.75 ||
This very cause is one, devoid of distinctions, and of the nature of pure consciousness.
From that, which is of the single form of Being and is conditioned by māyā, this universe arose. (1.76)
Some say that the cause is non-existent; yet the non-existent cannot possess causality.
Indeed, the power that produces the sprout is observed by everyone only when the seed exists. (1.77)
One who asserts that the cause is non-existent would accomplish his task by means of the son of a barren woman;
moreover, he might quench a great thirst by drinking the water of a mirage. (1.78)
Since this doctrine of non-existence is not possible according to either scripture or reasoning, therefore that which truly exists alone is the cause of all worlds. (1.79)
This supreme reality manifests as the form of the universe, as the forms of teacher and disciple, and it also appears in the form of the heart. 1.80.
The appearance of the world as real leads to the cycle of rebirth for those whose minds are immature;
therefore, the Upaniṣads establish that all this is unreal. (1.81)
For those best of men whose minds have reached maturity through their ancient good deeds,
he further awakens them with the realization that this entire world is Brahman.

Just as those who have not recognized gold perceive a golden ornament as being merely an ornament, so too, for people in this world who possess a lack of discernment, there is no truly real understanding.
O Brahmin, for whom could this, which is established as the very object of perception, be beyond direct experience?
Yet even that cannot be directly realized by the deluded who lack inquiry. 1.84
The entire world also constantly conducts its affairs by means of the two cognitions "I" and "this":
the first resides in the inner Self, while the last dwells in the body, the senses, and external objects. 1.85.

That notion of "I" regarding the body, the senses, and so forth, which have as their objects [the gross and subtle elements], is a great delusion; for that cognition of something as being what it is not is taught in the scriptures as *adhyāsa* (superimposition). (1.86)
Therefore, it is appropriate that the Supreme Self alone—the witness of all without exception—is the referent of "I.
This insentient ego-sense becomes manifest as if sentient only through its connection with the Existent (Sat). (1.87)
Therefore, in all bodies, that pure cognition which clearly shines forth as "I, I" has Brahman alone as its primary object. (1.88)
The meaning of the word "cow" is cowness (gotva), yet that [cowness] is also perceived as an individual object;
likewise, the supreme self (paramātman) is the referent of the word "I," yet through delusion it becomes the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). (1.89)
Just as the capacity to burn and other qualities of iron appear through contact with fire, so too do agency and other such attributes manifest in the "I" through association with consciousness. 1.90

Having realized that the true meaning of "I" is pure, incomparable, and non-dual, and distinct from the visible body, senses, and so forth, one should not conceive of anything as separate from it. 1.91.

Just as there is a multiplicity of pleasures and pains in the body due to the distinction of its parts, so too, even though there is no such distinction here, these selves possess a diversity of experiences. 1.92

"What is this? What is its nature? How did this come to be? What is its cause?"—the wise person should never contemplate [these questions] in this way; rather, the entire universe should be contemplated as being *māyā*. (1.93)
Just as wood disappears within a wooden artifact, and that artifact likewise disappears therein;
so too does the world disappear within the Supreme Self, and the Supreme Self disappears within the world. 1.94
On the great canvas consisting of the self, the Supreme Self, seeing by himself alone the manifold painting of the world drawn by himself, attains supreme joy. (1.95)

Pure consciousness alone—immaculate, undecaying, non-dual, blissful, and established in direct experience—is indeed Brahman; there is nothing else whatsoever. This is the certainty of the wise. (1.96)
This distinction between "knowledge" and "ignorance" is merely a conventional designation within worldly discourse.
From the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no such thing as reality at all; the Brahman alone exists, and nothing other than this exists.
If it is thought that there is something else, even that is established as being of the nature of this very existence;
for anything distinct from existence is proven to be empty by way of non-existence. (1.98)
Although that māyā has been sublated by the firmly established power of the realization of reality, it continues to appear even to these wise ones as their own self until the fall of the body. 1.99.
This is the distinction of the wise: even while perceiving the phenomenal world of saṃsāra, they do not perceive anything as separate from the Self, which is determined by all the Vedas. 1.100

What is to be contemplated and what is beyond contemplation? What is to be spoken and what is beyond speech? What is to be done and what is not to be done—all this is known by the wise who possess the heart of Brahman. 1.101.

For the wise who perceive every particular object of sight as being of the nature of pure vision, there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither the state of being the Supreme Self nor the state of being an individual soul. 1.102
This alone is the conclusion of all the Vedas—which have been repeatedly contemplated, whose own instructions are most unimpeded, and which reach the ultimate limit of authority. 1.103.
Thus enlightened by his teacher, that disciple was filled with joy; having prostrated at his feet, he reflected within himself upon the truth established through his own experience. (1.104)
I am ageless, I am imperishable, I am the wise one, I am the realization of the inner Self;
I am composed of supreme bliss, I am the Supreme Śiva, I exist as the all-pervading whole.
I am the primordial Self of all embodied beings; I am the one who relishes the experience of the bliss of the Self;
I am that whose greatness is experienced as "I" by everyone, from children to cowherds.
I am averse to the happiness of others; I am filled with the experience of the awakening to my own happiness;
I am far removed from this [world]; my mind is attached to pleasures other than [true] spiritual realization. (1.107)
I am the Lord of lords, free from attachment to envy and hatred;
I am devoted to providing the means for the attainment of the desired human goals for those whose minds are objects of my vision. 1.108.
I alone am the rising of the worlds; I am the Upanishad that creates the pleasure-garden of existence;
I am the flame of the sacrificial fire at the mouth of the submarine fire within the overflowing ocean of sorrow.
I am he who pervades above, below, and across with my own powerful majesty;
I am he who is perceived as having been accepted through the processes of reasoning, refutation, and investigation.
I am the seer, I am the multitude of seers; I am the vision, I am that which is seen.
I am prosperity, I am growth, I am contentment, and I am the radiance of the lamp of contentment.
I am the One; I am devoid of the duality that flashes forth as "this is such-and-such" or "it is thus.
I am to be sought through desirelessness; I am become the inner experience of the well-performed.
I am the illuminator of unity for those whose minds are purified by the thorough knowledge of the Great Saying;
I alone am the sovereign reality, the sun that destroys the delusion consisting mostly of the darkness of night.
I am the vigor of the medicinal herbs; I am that which weaves through and across the worlds as they expand;
I am the bee intoxicated by the fragrance of the bliss of the Self, shimmering with the essence of the syllable Om.
I am the medicine for all that is impure; I am free from the web of conditioned phenomena;
I am the supreme excellence of magnanimity; I am devoted to bestowing the various [attainments of] the four aims of life. (1.115)
I am the goad for all intoxicated lordly elephants by virtue of my greatness;
I am as stainless as the sky, and I am free from the transformations born of Śambara’s enemy (Kāma).
I am one who is understood through unerring instruction by those whose minds are free from the eightfold conceptualization;
I am averse to unstable pleasure and am fit for the attainment of the awakening to perfectly stable bliss.
I am filled with the essence of compassion; I have swallowed the world of Brahmā and the other gods;
I am distressed by the sight of impurity; and I am free from the taints of both sin and merit. || 1.118 ||
I am beyond the sphere of speech; I am transcendent of space; I am the source of the flower in the sky;
I am difficult for the wicked to approach; I am intent upon dispelling fragmentary knowledge.
I am one for whom the discourse of duality has dissolved; I am the primordial Brahman, the root of all that exists as embodied beings.
I am to be reached by those free from mental constructs; I am perfect consciousness, devoid of coming and going.
I am the mass of light that utterly destroys the dense veil of the darkness of profound delusion;
I am the distinction of time—whether it be a ghaṭikā, a day, a night, a year, a yuga, or a kalpa.
I am composed of both the moving and the unmoving; I am one whose conduct is praised for its clever intelligence;
I am difficult to traverse for fickle people; and I am the shore beyond the restless ocean of existence.

Rejoicing in the taste of the bliss of knowledge hidden within the ocean of Vedic meters, I am concealed from those whose minds are fixed on deceptive paths; I am accessible only through the path of peace. 1.123.
I am the fundamental source of the five great elements that constitute the domain of the lotus-seated goddess and others;
I am the bringer of bliss to the world, and I am free from birth, old age, death, and disease.
I am the diversity of various sounds—humming, roaring, tinkling, bellowing, and the manifold cries of the mouth;
I am the temple of the heart, illuminated by the lamp of self-knowledge that is instantly kindled.
I am knowledge, I am the object of knowledge, I am the knower, and I am the collection of means of knowledge;
yet, being devoid of knower, knowledge, and the object of knowledge, I am existence alone.
I am the state that transcends reality; I am bodiless, devoid of all objective existence;
I am difficult to be grasped by the ignorant; I am the Self, to be realized through the awakening of the meanings of the words "That" and "Thou," and I am compassion itself.
I am the gods, the Daityas, the night-stalkers, humans, animals, mountains, and so forth; I am devoid of body and senses; I am the divisions of the directions, such as the south-east and others.

I am composed of both dharma and adharma; yet I am free from the bondage of dharma, adharma, and the like. I am easily accessible to righteous people; I am blessed; I am the primordial source of the Creator.
I am devoid of name and the like; I am devoid of hell, heaven, and liberation;
I am not known by the beginning or the end; I am the essence of all the various Vedas.
I am one whose mind is purified by the knowledge of the ultimate truth that destroys the distinction between the lives of others and oneself;
I am nature, I am transformation, and I am the evolution of all fortunes.
I am the essence of the manifested world, sustained by the forms of the serpent, the mountain, and the elephant;
I am he who has vanquished the five-arrowed god with the fire of the eye arisen from the surface of his forehead.
I am not bound, yet even so I am not liberated from bondage;
I am not the object of awakening, I am not awakening itself, nor am I the awakener. (1.133)
I am devotion, I am worship, I am enjoyment, and I alone am both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
I am the ruler of all beings, and I am the root-source of the past, the present, and the future.
I am worthy of honor by the great, yet unworthy of honor by those of dull intellect;
I am difficult to attain for those whose minds are deluded by passion, pride, and infatuation, and who are burdened by evil latent tendencies.
I am the sacrifice, the sacrificer, the priest, and the ritual; I am devoid of death and the like.
I am the form of Yama, Varuṇa, Yakṣa, Vāsava, Rākṣasa, Marut, Īśa, and Agni.

I am he whose majesty is beheld through the playful observation of the training in the methods of protection; I am he established by the proof of manifest experience at the cessation of night and day. 1.137
I consist of the definition and the defined; I am the one characterized by definitions; I am devoid of dissolution and the like;
I consist of gain and loss; and though I am that which is to be attained, I am not being attained.
I am devoid of caste and stage of life; I consist of all castes; I am to be numbered among the most excellent;
I am beyond the range of speech, yet I am reached by the meaning of words.
I am unattainable even by hundreds of scriptures for those whose minds are devoid of tranquility and self-restraint;
yet I alone am the refuge for the wise, having shattered the multitude of their various doubts. 1.140
I am devoid of the six states of being; I am devoid of the six qualities; I am devoid of the six enemies;
I am devoid of the six sheaths; I am devoid of the web of the thirty-six principles.
I am composed of consciousness and bliss; I am the wish-fulfilling tree of meditative resolve;
I am free from the cycle of worldly existence; I am the direct realization of the knowledge of the Self. (1.142)
I am the sacrificial offering to the gods, I am the offering to the ancestors; I am devoid of the states of rejection and acceptance.
I am Hari, I am Hara, and I alone am Brahmā—the cause of them all.
I am he whose fear of impurity has been washed away; I am he who has destroyed the web of worldly afflictions through compassion;
I alone am the root of the various conventional expressions well-composed from the imperishable syllables beginning with *kṣa*.
What is the use of these many words? I alone am this entire universe of moving and unmoving things;
for indeed, spray, foam, and waves are not separate entities from the ocean.
Neither mother, nor father, nor sons, nor siblings, nor others provide refuge;
this alone shall be my supreme refuge: the feet placed upon my head by the Teacher. (1.146)
The feet of the Teacher remain present; his compassion remains unbounded in his gaze;
something ineffable remains in his word—what greater fulfillment of birth could there be than this?
The cooling glances from the feet of the venerable Guru—thick with the essence of compassion and like a wish-fulfilling tree for granting desired boons—pacify the fever of the mind. (1.148)
Having swallowed the restless mind and feeling profound satisfaction from the emergence of the great frog [of wisdom],
the single serpent composed of consciousness sleeps for a very long time within the cave of the heart.
In my vast ocean of blissful awakening, which contains the bubbles of world-systems,
he— having become a wind of illusion— appears again and again and then vanishes.
By the boat of the Guru’s compassion alone, propelled by the favorable wind of past merit, I have crossed the high ocean of saṃsāra with its unbearable waves of suffering. (1.151)
While darkness in the form of delusion prevailed, I saw this entire universe as "this is that"; but now that the sun of awakening has risen, I see nothing at all—what indeed is this wonder? (1.152)
Thus, reflecting repeatedly with joy upon the attainment of self-knowledge, one indeed reaches the supreme state of absolute liberation at the conclusion of the karma that has already begun. 1.153.
Let the virtuous reflect within upon this treatise, which dispels the darkness of delusion, enables the crossing of the surging ocean of saṃsāra, and reveals the nature of one's own self. 1.154.
Thus [ends] the work of the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas.
The exposition of one's own self is complete.
